text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Monday he supported the elections that dealt Mexico's ruling party its worst defeat in seven decades, calling the democratic vote "good for our common future".

Elections in Mexico on Sunday broke the 68-year-old grip of President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) on the lower house of Congress. The PRI was also trounced in the first race for Mexico City mayor this century.

"We support the elections and we support the expression of popular will for the people of Mexico," Clinton said during an exchange with reporters in Madrid, where he arrived to attend a two-day NATO summit that begins on Tuesday.

"The United States wants to be a good partner and a good friend. We share a long border, we share a common heritage ... we believe that anything that adds to Mexico's strength as a democracy is good for our common future," he said.
He said the elections "gave the Mexican people an opportunity for an open free expression of their will".

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, also in Madrid for the NATO summit, told reporters: "It is our custom that we respect the votes of the people in countries where they elect their legislatures or their presidents."
"We also have quite a lot of experience in dealing with countries where there is divided government, including our own," she added.
Zedillo, whose policies have been heavily backed by the United States despite major economic and drug problems in Mexico, was not up for reelection.
